## Recap: the three claims from Lecture 2A {.smaller}

1. A recorded category can hide a **distribution of possible responses**.
2. Dependence means different things within a fixed sentence and across random
   sentences.
3. Expected Brier score separates **forecast mismatch** from **label
   variability**.

Today we will repeat each idea with concrete sentences and numbers, then use the
same workflow in the lab.

## First hold one sentence fixed {.smaller}

For one fixed sentence:

> “The service was fine.”

- Repeat the measurement by drawing new raters.
- The sentence stays fixed; rater responses vary.

**Question:** are responses independent conditional on this sentence?

**Answer:** not necessarily. Conditional independence is a modeling assumption;
separate raters make it plausible, but a shared discussion, instructions, or context
could make their responses dependent.

## Then let the sentence change {.smaller}

Across a benchmark:

- Draw a new sentence $X$.
- Collect multiple responses to that sentence.
- Repeat with another sentence.

**Question:** are the responses independent across randomly sampled sentences?

**Answer:** not generally. Even if responses are independent conditional on each
sentence, the shared random sentence $X$ can make them marginally dependent.

**Different repeated experiment, different independence claim.**

## Three categories create two kinds of dependence {.smaller}

For rater $i$, write the one-hot response as

$$T_i=(T_{i-},T_{i0},T_{i+}),\qquad T_{i-}+T_{i0}+T_{i+}=1.$$

**Between raters:** for a fixed sentence, we might assume

$$T_1\perp T_2\mid X=x.$$

**Within one rater:** the three indicators cannot be independent. If
$q(x)=(.20,.50,.30)$, then

$$\operatorname{Cov}(T_{i0},T_{i+}\mid X=x)=0-(.50)(.30)=-.15.$$

Independent raters do **not** imply independent category indicators.

## A changing sentence can create positive or negative dependence {.smaller .compact-table}

Suppose A and B are equally likely and two raters are independent conditional on
the sentence.

| Sentence $X$ | $q_0(X)$ | $q_+(X)$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| A: clear praise | $.15$ | $.80$ |
| B: mixed review | $.65$ | $.20$ |

Across sentences,

$$\operatorname{Cov}(T_{1+},T_{2+})=\operatorname{Var}\{q_+(X)\}=.09,$$

while

$$\operatorname{Cov}(T_{10},T_{2+})=\operatorname{Cov}\{q_0(X),q_+(X)\}=-.075.$$

The sign depends on which response probabilities move together across $X$.

## Keep five votes attached to one sentence {.smaller}

For one DynaSent sentence $j$:

> “I waited only twenty minutes this time.”

$$
(L_{j1},\ldots,L_{j5})=(-,-,-,0,0)
$$

$$
N_j=(3,2,0),\qquad \widehat q_j=(.60,.40,0),\qquad
\text{majority}_j=-.
$$

- **One** sentence is the evaluation unit.
- **Five** labels are its repeated measurements.
- The vote counts, fractions, and majority are summaries of that same record.

The lab begins by constructing this sentence-level representation.

## The protocol changes what the label measures {.smaller}

Text:

> “The camera is tiny, but the battery lasts all day.”

**Protocol A:** label the overall sentiment.

**Protocol B:** label mixed praise and criticism as neutral unless one side
clearly dominates.

The text did not change. The measurement rule did—and the response distribution
can change with it.

Before averaging votes, ask whether all raters received the same question,
instructions, and context.

## DynaSent has two item-construction processes {.smaller .compact-table}

| Round | How sentences entered validation |
|---|---|
| 1 | Naturally occurring Yelp sentences selected because an initial model found them challenging |
| 2 | Workers edited Yelp prompts to fool a newer model trained using Round 1 |

Both rounds then used five-person validation.

Round 2 is not a randomized treatment applied to Round 1 sentences. A round
comparison is descriptive: it compares two constructed item populations.

You will compare the rounds descriptively in the lab, then explain how their
construction affects the target in Homework 2, Problem 2.

::: notes
[Sources]
- Potts et al. (2021), DynaSent: https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.186/
:::

## Keep the five votes visible during EDA {.smaller .compact-table}

For each sentence, compute

$$N_k=\sum_{i=1}^5T_{ik},\qquad \widehat q_k=N_k/5.$$

| Votes $(N_-,N_0,N_+)$ | Majority | What the majority hides |
|:---:|:---:|---|
| $(5,0,0)$ | negative | unanimous judgment |
| $(3,2,0)$ | negative | a nearby neutral boundary |
| $(3,0,2)$ | negative | polarized sentiment judgments |

All three have the same majority class. They are not the same measurement
outcome.

In the lab, these patterns guide which sentences you inspect closely.

## Read a 3–2 split with the sentence {.smaller}

Suppose the votes are $(3,2,0)$ for

> “I waited only twenty minutes this time.”

The count tells us **that** raters disagreed. The sentence can suggest **why**:

- “only” may signal improvement;
- twenty minutes may still be a complaint;
- “this time” invokes missing prior context.

This is purposeful case inspection. It suggests mechanisms; it does not estimate
how common each mechanism is.

## Worked Brier example: hold the forecast fixed {.smaller}

Use class order negative, neutral, positive. Five votes are

$$N=(0,2,3),$$

and the model forecast is

$$p=(0.10,0.35,0.55).$$

The same measurements produce two targets:

$$t_{\text{hard}}=(0,0,1),\qquad
t_{\text{soft}}=(0,0.40,0.60).$$

**Next:** score the same forecast against each target.

## Against the hard target, the score is $0.335$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B(p,t_{\text{hard}})
&=(.10-0)^2+(.35-0)^2+(.55-1)^2\\
&=.010+.1225+.2025\\
&=0.335.
\end{aligned}
$$

The majority rule turns the target into “positive with probability 1.” It
discards both neutral votes.

## Against the soft target, the score is $0.015$

$$
\begin{aligned}
B(p,t_{\text{soft}})
&=(.10-0)^2+(.35-.40)^2+(.55-.60)^2\\
&=.010+.0025+.0025\\
&=0.015.
\end{aligned}
$$

The forecast did not change. The soft target preserved the observed $2/5$–$3/5$
split.

## What did the lower Brier score mean? {.smaller}

It did **not** show that the model suddenly improved.

It showed that the model forecast was much closer to the empirical vote
distribution than to the one-hot majority target.

Report:

1. what information the hard target discarded;
2. how many measurements formed the soft target;
3. whether conclusions about model performance changed.

Neither target is automatically “the truth.”

The lab repeats this comparison on the data; Homework 2, Problem 1 explains its
expected value.

## Align the forecasters by sentence {.smaller .compact-table}

For every sampled sentence $X_j$, record all three forecasts on the same row:

| Sentence | Model A | Model B | Student |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $X_1$: clear praise | $p_A(X_1)$ | $p_B(X_1)$ | $p_S(X_1)$ |
| $X_2$: mixed review | $p_A(X_2)$ | $p_B(X_2)$ | $p_S(X_2)$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ |

The **rows** may be iid if the sentences $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ are sampled iid and
each forecasting procedure stays fixed.

The three entries within a row are **not three iid rater draws**:

- not identically distributed: A, B, and the student use different procedures;
- not justified as independent: all three forecasts are functions of the same
  sentence $X_j$.

They are paired comparisons on each sentence. Homework 2, Problem 3 asks you to
use this structure with actual forecasts.

## The lab repeats this workflow in six moves {.smaller}

1. Make personal sentiment measurements before seeing the votes.
2. Construct vote fractions and agreement patterns.
3. Inspect random, unanimous, and 3–2 cases with their sentences.
4. Compare the two construction rounds descriptively.
5. Score one forecast against hard and soft targets.
6. State which iid and exchangeability assumptions are—or are not—justified.

Every highlighted work box in the notebook requires a response or code edit.

## Homework formalizes the same examples {.smaller}

- **Problem 1:** derive expected Brier score for one label and for an averaged
  soft target.
- **Problem 2:** explain how aggregation and item selection construct a
  benchmark target.
- **Problem 3:** compare three forecasters against two measured targets and
  explain why they are not iid, interchangeable raters.

**Recurring distinction:** a label, an average of labels, and a majority target
are different statistical objects.
